claims.statement: frontend/mcm-app/server.js is the BFF's production entrypoint: a CommonJS Express adapter that requires `expo-server/adapter/express`, hands the exported dist/server bundle to `createRequestHandler({ build: DIST_SERVER })`, and serves dist/client as static assets; because it runs outside the Metro bundle it cannot require anything from src/, which is why scheduled work reaches the bundle through a loopback HTTP call instead of a function call.

server.js pre-seeds `globalThis.__ExpoImportMetaRegistry = { url: pathToFileURL(__filename).href }` before createRequestHandler loads the bundle, because Metro rewrites `import.meta.url` in bundled dependencies to `globalThis.__ExpoImportMetaRegistry.url` and the exported `expo-server` runtime — unlike the Metro dev server — never populates that registry; the `if (!globalThis.__ExpoImportMetaRegistry)` guard is intentional so a future expo-server version that populates it makes the line a no-op rather than being clobbered.

Without the registry seeding, any bundled dependency calling `createRequire(import.meta.url)` — @copilotkit/runtime's lazily-required adapter on the /bff-api/agent/run path — throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'url')` asynchronously inside the streaming respond pipeline, so the route's own try/catch never sees it: the client hangs with no 500 and no log line, in the container only.

The same lazy require is a build-time consequence: because the specifier is a bare string passed to createRequire(globalThis.__ExpoImportMetaRegistry.url), a static closure walk cannot see it, so the BFF image build re-derives the dynamic specifiers from the freshly exported dist/server and fails when one is not accounted for in the prune script's known-specifier map.

Under express 5 (path-to-regexp v8) the Expo catch-all must be the named, braced route `'/{*splat}'`: a bare `'*'` is rejected at BOOT with `Missing parameter name at index 1: *` while routes are being registered, so the process never reaches app.listen, and the braces make the wildcard optional so `/` itself still matches.

The catch-all uses `app.all` rather than `app.use` deliberately: a route decodes its params, so a malformed percent-encoded path such as `/bff-api/%E0%A4%A` is answered 400 by express before the Expo handler sees it, and the single registration forwards every method and the raw query string (bracket syntax included) for both the /bff-api API surface and the SSR pages.

Static serving selects between two express.static instances on the last DECODED segment of the request path (a dotfile-last path goes to the default `ignore` instance, everything else to a `dotfiles: 'allow'` one), and an undecodable path falls to the strict instance — so a dotfile inside a dot-directory is not served, `/%2Eenv` counts as a dotfile because send decodes before it checks, and files inside dot-directories are served.

serve-static 2 (express 5) changed the `dotfiles` default to ignore files INSIDE a dot-directory as well, which would silently 404 the 45 dependency-shipped assets `expo export` writes under `dist/client/assets/node_modules/.pnpm/…` — the Outfit brand fonts and expo-router's icons — so express 4's rule (ignore only a path whose last segment is a dotfile) is deliberately reproduced by the two-instance selection.

Two suites boot the real `server.js` in a child process, and together they are the only tests that exercise the express hosting layer, but since feature 087 they do NOT share a stubbed adapter: `tests/unit/bff-server-adapter.test.ts` (the pin for the catch-all, param decoding, static serving and the header middleware) copies the real `server.js` and `web-security-headers.js` into a temp directory beside a fixture `dist/client` and boots it with `node -r tests/unit/fixtures/expo-adapter-stub.cjs`, a `Module._load` hook that replaces only `expo-server/adapter/express` with a handler echoing what express delivered to it — the stub no longer echoes an origin, because its `X-Test-Origin` echo claimed to mirror the adapter and is how a green suite hid item #843 — while `tests/unit/bff-server-trust-proxy.test.ts` boots the same real `server.js` with no stub at all, against the real adapter. `express` resolves from the package's own `node_modules` via `NODE_PATH`, so the version under test is the declared one; the unit tier imports TS modules and the integration tier calls route handlers, and both bypass `server.js`.

No other test would catch the font-serving regression: tests/e2e/web/font-fallback.spec.ts deliberately aborts every web-font request and asserts the app still renders on the system fallback, so it passes whether or not the real fonts are servable from dist/client.

CopilotKit's React Native runtime issues its /bff-api/agent/run request through its own XMLHttpRequest-based streaming-fetch polyfill, which never passes through the axios instance's response interceptor (utils/api-client.ts) or the token-refresh module behind it, so a 401 on the run has no interceptor to recover it and the refresh-and-retry has to live at the fetch level; cookie delivery works only because React Native's XMLHttpRequest defaults `withCredentials` to true — the polyfill itself does not set init.credentials — so a future RN or CopilotKit upgrade that changes that default breaks cookie delivery silently, with the Android E2E harness as the intended regression net.

src/utils/agent-fetch-refresh.ts wraps `globalThis.fetch` once (idempotently, no-op where fetch is unavailable) so that a 401 on the agent run route triggers silentRefresh() followed by a single retry with the fresh cookie; the wrapper is installed by the assistant polyfill loader — the first import in app/_layout.tsx — before CopilotKit issues any run, and CopilotKit resolves fetch at call time.

A second, distinct recovery in the same wrapper handles a THROWN transport error on the agent route only: it waits RUN_RETRY_DELAY_MS (250 ms) for a reset tunnel to re-establish and retries exactly once; non-agent throws propagate unchanged and a genuine 4xx returns a Response so it is never retried. The source justifies the single retry by asserting that a dropped connection aborts the upstream gateway turn through the adapter's AbortController, making the cut turn idempotent-on-failure — but that rationale is asserted rather than measured: feature 087's research records that the express entry does not pass the abort `signal` the plain `http` entry does, and that the new adapter's `respond` guards `writableEnded`/`destroyed`, so whether this failure still surfaces in the same shape is an open reading to take from current counts, per the E2E runbook's standing lesson on `Cannot pipe to a closed or destroyed stream`. What is pinned is the bound: one retry, in code and in the unit suite.

Neither recovery loops: a still-401 response after a successful refresh is returned as-is, a failed refresh returns the original 401 with no retry, and a second consecutive throw is propagated — so the 401 path and the transport-drop path are each capped at one retry, and createRefreshingFetch is a pure factory taking an injected baseFetch + refresh so both paths are unit-tested without any global.

assistant-polyfills.native.ts is ordered so the refresh wrapper is installed after the CopilotKit crypto and streaming polyfills and before any CopilotKit run — the crypto polyfill, then @copilotkit/react-native/polyfills, then installAgentFetchRefresh() — and its `require` calls are deliberately inline rather than hoisted imports so the LogBox ignore for the crypto polyfill's import-time warning is registered first; the order must not be changed.

The web and native assistant-polyfill loaders are deliberately split at the platform boundary for bundle size: the unsuffixed assistant-polyfills.ts is the web variant and installs ONLY the refresh wrapper (the crypto/streaming globals are native on web), while assistant-polyfills.native.ts loads the polyfill libraries — whose static requires otherwise put text-encoding (535 KB) and web-streams-polyfill (61 KB) in the entry chunk for every web user even though they can never execute there.

Verification of the agent transport's recovery is split by tier. The web E2E tests/e2e/web/agent-session-refresh.spec.ts no longer stages a client-side expiry — there is no token cookie to drop — and instead ages the session's server-held access token to expired in the dev BFF's Redis store through tests/e2e/web/setup/bff-session-store.ts, which is possible because the expiry times sit in clear beside the sealed tokens; it then asserts the renewal is transparent: the protected route still answers 200 with no 401 and no token cookie set, the expiry moved forward, and POST /bff-api/auth/refresh succeeds on the session cookie alone and re-sets only mcm_session_id. The client-side orchestration of a 401 → refresh → retry over a real refused run, and the RN-default cookie delivery, still rest on the Android harness.

The public-scheme trap: `expo-server`'s express entry builds each request as `new URL(req.url, `${proto}://${req.headers.host}`)` with `proto` derived from `socket.encrypted`, so behind the TLS-terminating proxy it is always `http` and express's `req.protocol` is ignored by the adapter. Before feature 087 that meant the two routes deriving an OAuth callback from `new URL(req.url).origin` — the backup consent callback and the account-deletion re-authentication callback (feature 076) — sent Keycloak an unregistered `http://` redirect_uri, which Keycloak refused with `Invalid parameter: redirect_uri` (measured in production 2026-10-25, item 843). CI and dev never saw it because there the BFF serves HTTPS itself on `:8443`, which is why the behaviour is pinned by a unit suite that boots the real `server.js` against the real adapter rather than by the web E2E run.

One half of the public-scheme fix is `app.set('trust proxy', 1)`, applied at boot above the routes and only when `TRUSTED_PROXY === 'true'`. A numeric value compiles to a hop-count predicate over the socket hop index, so `1` trusts exactly the immediate peer (the tunnel) and nothing wider — the narrowest form that still describes a one-hop deployment, where `true` would trust any peer including a directly connecting client and an address list or CIDR would have to be maintained; gating it on the env var is what keeps the setting from ever being stronger than the deployment actually is. It is not sufficient on its own: the adapter takes the scheme from the socket, so `server.js` must also make `req.url` absolute in the catch-all before the handler sees it.

Only the SCHEME can move when `trust proxy` is enabled: it makes `req.protocol` honour a trusted hop's `X-Forwarded-Proto`, but the origin `server.js` hands the adapter is built with `req.get('host')`, a raw `Host` header read with no proxy logic, so `X-Forwarded-Host` cannot change the origin a callback is derived from. The suite pins this directly, through the real adapter — a request with `X-Forwarded-Proto: https` and `X-Forwarded-Host: attacker.test` still yields the origin built from the raw `Host`.

Unset must stay unset, and unset is the default: `TRUSTED_PROXY` defaults to `false` in `src/config/env.ts`, so a directly exposed BFF keeps ignoring a client-supplied `X-Forwarded-Proto` and cannot be talked into believing it serves `https`; production is the deployment that sets it (`TRUSTED_PROXY: "true"` in `compose.prod.yaml`, for the same proxy rather than for this fix). The same variable has a second, independent consumer inside the bundle — the rate-limit client identity that `extractClientIp` derives from the right-most `X-Forwarded-For` hop (feature 009, finding #4) — so setting `trust proxy` in `server.js` does not change rate-limit identity, and `extractClientIp` does not change the scheme.

Since feature 085 the member's access and refresh tokens are held by the BFF, sealed beside the Redis session, so requireAuth renews a nearly expired access token on the very request that needs it and an access-token expiry mid-session no longer reaches the client at all; the client's only credential is the opaque `mcm_session_id` cookie, and the retired `mcm_access_token` / `mcm_refresh_token` cookies are never read, only ever cleared. A `/bff-api/agent/run` 401 therefore now means the session or its run-scoped identity was refused — in practice `401 AGENT_IDENTITY_REJECTED` from a refused subject-token mint — rather than an expired client-held token, which is what the wrapper's silentRefresh() + one-retry answers.

The wrapper refreshes only on a 401 and passes a 503 straight through, which the BFF's refusal vocabulary makes load-bearing: `401 AGENT_IDENTITY_REJECTED` means Keycloak rejected the member's credential (renew once, then sign in) while a retryable `503 AGENT_IDENTITY_UNAVAILABLE` means Keycloak was unreachable or erroring — including a misconfigured exchange client's `403 access_denied` — and an outage is not a reason to touch the member's session. The unit suite pins this with a mutation test: making the wrapper refresh on 503 turns that case red.

CopilotKit reports a refused `/run` through its `onError` subscription, never as a rejected promise, and for a non-2xx response the error's message IS the response body — so src/components/agent/assistant-run-failure.ts decodes the BFF's `code` and picks the member-facing text: the session-ending codes (AGENT_IDENTITY_REJECTED, REFRESH_FAILED, SESSION_NOT_FOUND, SESSION_EXPIRED, SESSION_IDLE_TIMEOUT, SESSION_ABSOLUTE_TIMEOUT, UNAUTHORIZED) read 'Your session has expired. Please sign in again.' and the retryable set (AGENT_IDENTITY_UNAVAILABLE, KEYCLOAK_UNAVAILABLE, SESSION_RENEWAL_PENDING) reads 'The assistant is temporarily unavailable. Please try again.', with a generic fallback that names no internals — where before 085 a failed turn showed the member nothing at all.

Feature 087 replaced the unmaintained `@expo/server` package with `expo-server`: `server.js` requires `expo-server/adapter/express` and creates the handler with `createRequestHandler({ build: DIST_SERVER })` (the old adapter's `mode` option no longer exists), and `expo-server` is a direct dependency of `mcm-app` pinned to the version `expo-router` already resolves, which matters because it is also one of the two prune roots the BFF image's dependency-closure walk starts from (`STATIC_ROOTS = ['express', 'expo-server']`) and a missing root fails the image build rather than the running app. Any surviving reference to `@expo/server` in a manifest, prune root or stub is history.

The second half of the public-scheme fix lives in the catch-all: `server.js` rewrites `req.url` to `${req.protocol}://${req.get('host')}${req.url}` immediately before calling the expo-server handler, so the adapter's own base URL — built from the socket scheme — becomes irrelevant; this is the only hook the adapter offers, and removing the wrapper must turn the `https` rows of `tests/unit/bff-server-trust-proxy.test.ts` red, which is how feature 087 verified the change. `tests/unit/bff-server-adapter.test.ts` correspondingly asserts that its handler now receives that absolute URL, built from the request's own `Host`.

`tests/unit/bff-server-trust-proxy.test.ts` stubs nothing on its path: it boots the real `server.js` beside `tests/unit/fixtures/real-adapter-build`, a minimal `dist/server` holding `_expo/routes.json` with empty `htmlRoutes` and `notFoundRoutes` plus one API route whose function returns `Response.json({ url: request.url })`, and asserts the URL that route actually received for the four rows of the hosting contract (trusted proxy with `X-Forwarded-Proto`, with and without a forwarded host, and no trusted proxy). Because the fixture encodes the SDK's manifest shape, an SDK change that breaks it fails the suite — the intended prompt rather than silent drift.

A harness that re-implements the behaviour it is checking is not a pin: the stub the scheme suite used until feature 087 computed and echoed the request origin itself (`X-Test-Origin`), so the assertion tested the stub's belief about the adapter rather than the adapter's behaviour and stayed green while production refused the `http://` callback; feature 087 deleted that echo, moved the scheme assertion onto the real adapter, and left the stub only where the subject genuinely is the express layer in front of the handler.
